title: Magnetic Effect of Electric Current
summary: The ancient Greeks found lodestone, a natural magnet (an iron oxide, Fe3O4) that attracts iron. Natural magnets are weak, so strong artificial (permanent) magnets are made in many shapes — bar, horseshoe, cylindrical, circular, rectangular — and used in motors, loudspeakers, microphones, door bells, headphones and generators. Properties: a magnet attracts iron (most strongly at its poles); a freely suspended magnet always rests in the north–south direction (north pole and south pole); like poles repel and unlike poles attract; iron brought near a magnet becomes a magnet itself; the poles cannot be separated — each broken piece is a complete magnet.

The region around a magnet in which a compass needle experiences a force (torque) is its magnetic field. It is shown by magnetic lines of force: they start at the north pole and end at the south pole outside the magnet; they never intersect; and they are crowded near the poles, where the field is strongest. The tangent at any point gives the field direction. The earth behaves like a giant bar magnet (because of currents in its molten iron core); its magnetic poles are tilted about 11° from the geographic poles, so a compass needle points roughly north–south and helps navigation.

In 1820 H.C. Oersted found that a compass needle near a current-carrying wire is deflected: an electric current produces a magnetic field around it. A larger current gives a larger deflection, reversing the current reverses the deflection, and stopping the current removes it. The field around a straight wire is in circles; its direction is given by the right-hand thumb rule — hold the wire in the right hand with the thumb along the current, and the curled fingers show the direction of the field.

A solenoid is a long coil of insulated wire. When current flows through it, it behaves like a bar magnet, with field lines like those of a bar magnet (parallel lines inside). With a soft iron core inside, it becomes an electromagnet, because the iron's atoms line up and strengthen the field. The strength of an electromagnet depends on the current, the number of turns and the nature of the core. Compared with a bar magnet (permanent, fixed strength and poles, weaker), an electromagnet is temporary (magnetic only while current flows), its strength can be changed by changing the current, its poles can be reversed by reversing the current, and it can be made very strong. Uses: electric bells, motors, generators, cranes, MRI machines, brakes of fast trains, particle accelerators.

Electric bell: pressing the button completes the circuit, the U-shaped electromagnet attracts the soft-iron armature and the hammer strikes the gong; this breaks the circuit at the contact screw, the electromagnet loses its magnetism and the spring pulls the armature back, remaking the circuit — so the hammer strikes repeatedly while the button is pressed.

A current-carrying wire placed in a magnetic field experiences a force (studied by Faraday); it is greatest when the wire is perpendicular to the field and reverses when the current or the field is reversed. Fleming's left-hand rule: stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the left hand mutually perpendicular — if the forefinger points along the field and the middle finger along the current, the thumb gives the direction of the force (motion). This force is the principle of the electric motor, which changes electrical energy into mechanical energy (fans, mixers, washing machines, cranes).

Michael Faraday (1831) discovered that a changing magnetic field linked with a coil produces (induces) a current in it — electromagnetic induction. Moving a magnet into or out of a coil connected to a galvanometer makes the needle deflect, in opposite directions for in and out; the faster the movement, the larger the current. Similarly, changing the current in one coil induces a current in a nearby coil. Generators and transformers work on this principle; Fleming's right-hand rule gives the direction of the induced current.

A generator changes mechanical energy into electrical energy. AC generator: a rectangular coil (ABCD) rotates between the poles of a strong magnet; its ends are joined to two slip rings with brushes. As the coil turns, the magnetic field through it changes continuously and the induced current reverses its direction every half rotation — alternating current (AC). The current produced depends on the number of turns, the strength of the magnetic field and the speed of rotation (also the area of the coil). DC generator: the slip rings are replaced by a split-ring commutator, which reverses the connections every half turn, so the current in the outer circuit flows in one direction — direct current (DC), suitable for charging batteries.

A battery gives DC, which flows in one direction; mains supply is AC, which changes direction periodically. In India the frequency is 50 Hz: the current completes 50 cycles each second (changing direction 100 times), so frequency is quoted for AC but not for DC. AC is preferred for supply because its voltage can be stepped up or down with transformers, so it is transmitted at high voltage and low current with little loss, and AC machines are robust; transformers do not work with DC. DC is needed for electroplating and electrolysis, charging batteries and making electromagnets. A rectifier changes AC to DC. DC of the same voltage is more dangerous, because a person cannot let go of it.

Power stations generate AC at about 11 kV and 50 Hz; step-up transformers raise it to 132 kV or more for transmission, and step-down transformers lower it to 220 V for homes. Two wires come into a house: the live (phase) wire, usually red, at 220 V, and the neutral wire (black) at zero; a third, the earth wire (green), is connected to a copper plate buried in the ground. Appliances are joined in parallel. Accidents are caused by current leakage (worn insulation), short circuit (live and neutral touching) and overloading (too many appliances on one circuit). Safety devices: the fuse — a wire of tin–lead alloy with high resistance and low melting point, connected in series in the live wire, which melts when the current is too large (5 A for lighting, 15 A for power circuits); the miniature circuit breaker (MCB), a switch that trips automatically on overload or short circuit; and earthing of metal bodies of appliances, which carries leaked current safely to the ground. Precautions: switch off the main switch before repairs or in emergencies; never touch live wires; separate a shock victim using a dry non-conductor; never pour water on an electrical fire; use ISI-marked wires and fittings; a tester shows whether a point is live.

objective: Fill in the blanks: The production of an electric current by a changing magnetic field is called ________, and it was discovered by ________.

case.passage: During a physics lab, students used two types of generators. One had a rotating coil connected to slip rings; the other had a rotating coil connected to a commutator. With an ammeter they noticed that the current in the first generator reversed again and again, and that how often it reversed depended on the rotation speed of the coil. The instructor explained that the first is an AC (alternating current) generator and the second a DC (direct current) generator.

vsa: What is a solenoid? Draw the magnetic field pattern of a current-carrying solenoid.

A solenoid is a long cylindrical coil of many turns of insulated wire. When current flows, its field is like that of a bar magnet: inside, the lines are straight, parallel and close together (a strong, uniform field); outside, they curve from one end (N) to the other (S).

or: What is an electric generator? Name its two types.
A device that changes mechanical energy into electrical energy by electromagnetic induction. Types: AC generator and DC generator.

vsa: Write two differences between a bar magnet and an electromagnet.

(1) A bar magnet is permanent; an electromagnet is magnetic only while current flows. (2) A bar magnet's strength and poles are fixed; an electromagnet's strength can be changed by changing the current and its poles reversed by reversing the current (it can also be made much stronger).
What is the function of the earth wire? Why should electrical appliances be earthed?

The earth wire connects the metal body of an appliance to the earth. If current leaks to the body, it flows through this low-resistance path into the ground instead of through a person touching it, preventing a dangerous shock.

Stretch the thumb, forefinger and middle finger of the left hand so that they are mutually perpendicular. If the forefinger points in the direction of the magnetic field and the middle finger in the direction of the current, the thumb points in the direction of the force (motion) on the conductor.
Name three causes of accidents due to electricity.
Leakage of current through damaged insulation, short circuit (live and neutral wires touching) and overloading of a circuit.
Two coils A and B are placed close to each other. If the current in coil A is changed, will a current be induced in coil B? Give reason.
Yes. Changing the current in A changes its magnetic field, so the field linked with coil B changes; this induces a current in B (electromagnetic induction).
sa: Why is alternating current (AC) used more widely than direct current (DC) for industrial and domestic purposes? Give two reasons. Represent AC and DC graphically.

(1) AC voltage can be stepped up or down with transformers, so it can be transmitted over long distances at high voltage and low current with little loss. (2) AC machines (motors, generators) are simpler and more robust. Graphs: DC — a horizontal straight line (constant current against time); AC — a wave going above and below the time axis (current rising, falling and reversing regularly).
(a) Explain why AC is preferred to DC for transmission from a power plant to local distribution centres. (b) Name two processes that can take place with DC only.

(a) AC can be stepped up to a very high voltage by transformers, which lowers the current and therefore the heating loss in transmission lines; at the other end it is stepped down for use. DC cannot be transformed, so its losses would be large. (b) Electroplating/electrolysis and charging of batteries (also making electromagnets).
What is electromagnetic induction? Describe an activity to show it.

Electromagnetic induction is the production of current in a coil when the magnetic field linked with it changes. Activity: connect a coil of insulated copper wire to a galvanometer. Move a bar magnet quickly into the coil — the needle deflects; pull it out — it deflects the other way; hold it still — no deflection. Moving it faster gives a larger deflection.
How does an electric bell work?

It has a U-shaped electromagnet, a soft-iron armature with a hammer, a gong and a contact screw. Pressing the switch completes the circuit; the electromagnet attracts the armature and the hammer strikes the gong. The armature then leaves the contact screw, breaking the circuit, so the electromagnet loses its magnetism and a spring pulls the armature back, completing the circuit again. This repeats rapidly, and the bell rings while the switch is pressed.
(a) What does the direction of the thumb indicate in the right-hand thumb rule? How is this rule different from Fleming's left-hand rule? (b) Draw a labelled circuit diagram of a DC generator.

(a) Holding a straight current-carrying wire in the right hand, the thumb points in the direction of the current and the curled fingers give the direction of the magnetic field around it. Fleming's left-hand rule instead gives the direction of the force on a conductor placed in an external magnetic field (thumb = force, forefinger = field, middle finger = current). (b) A rectangular coil rotating between the N and S poles of a magnet, its ends joined to the two halves of a split-ring commutator, with two carbon brushes touching the halves and connected to an external circuit with a galvanometer/bulb.
la: What is meant by electromagnetic induction? Describe an activity to show that a current is set up in a closed coil when the magnetic field passing through it changes. State the factors on which the induced current depends, and name two devices based on this principle.

Electromagnetic induction is the production of an electric current in a conductor when the magnetic field linked with it changes. Activity: wind many turns of insulated copper wire on a cardboard tube and join the ends to a galvanometer. Push a strong bar magnet into the coil — the galvanometer deflects; hold it still — no deflection; pull it out — it deflects the other way. Moving the magnet faster gives more deflection. The induced current depends on the rate of change of the magnetic field (speed of motion), the strength of the magnet and the number of turns in the coil. Devices: electric generator (dynamo) and transformer.
Explain the principle of an AC generator and draw a labelled diagram. On what factors does the current generated depend? What is meant by 220 V, 50 Hz AC?

Principle: electromagnetic induction — when a coil rotates in a magnetic field, the magnetic field through it changes continuously and a current is induced. Diagram: a rectangular coil ABCD on an axle between the N and S poles of a strong magnet, its ends joined to two slip rings with brushes connected to an external circuit. As the coil rotates, the induced current increases, decreases and reverses every half turn, so alternating current flows. The current depends on the number of turns, the strength of the magnetic field, the speed of rotation (and the area of the coil). 220 V, 50 Hz means the supply has a voltage of 220 V and completes 50 cycles each second (changing direction 100 times).

(a) State the principle of a generator and draw a labelled diagram of a DC generator. (b) What changes should be made to increase the current it produces? (c) Why do we mention the frequency of AC but not of DC?

(a) Principle: electromagnetic induction. A DC generator has a rectangular coil rotating between the poles of a magnet; its ends are joined to the two halves of a split-ring commutator with brushes, which reverse the connections every half turn so the current in the external circuit always flows in one direction. (b) Use more turns in the coil, a stronger magnet, rotate the coil faster (and use a larger coil). (c) AC changes direction periodically, so it has a frequency (cycles per second, 50 Hz in India). DC flows steadily in one direction and does not reverse, so it has no frequency.
